course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Expanding Democracy
lesson.summary: How voting expanded from property owners to nearly all adult white men between 1800 and 1848, how party politics changed as a result, and who was left out.
learningGoals: Explain how and why suffrage expanded for white men.
Explain how party organization and campaigning changed as more people voted.
Explain how race and sex limited the expansion of democracy.
lesson.bigIdea: Political participation grew sharply for white men, but the same decades narrowed or denied the vote for women, free African Americans, and American Indians.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of the expansion of participatory democracy. Always ask who gained a political voice, why, and who was excluded.

sections.title: Ending property requirements

blocks.text: The nation's transition to a more participatory democracy was achieved by expanding suffrage from a system based on property ownership to one based on voting by all adult white men. At the nation's founding, most states required voters to own property or pay taxes. New western states, such as Indiana, Illinois, and Missouri, entered the Union with few or no property requirements. Older states revised their constitutions, and by the 1840s most states had dropped property requirements for white men.

Several developments explained the change. Many wage earners owned no land, and they argued that men who paid taxes and served in the militia should have a voice in government. Competing parties sought new voters, and the idea that the common man should have political influence became part of political life. In Rhode Island, which still used its colonial charter and limited the vote to landowners, Thomas Dorr led a movement in 1841–1842 that pressed for broader suffrage, and the state adopted a new constitution in 1843.

sections.takeaway: Property requirements fell as western states, wage earners, and competing parties pressed for the vote.

sections.title: Party politics and participation

blocks.text: The expansion of voting was accompanied by the growth of political parties. Parties nominated candidates at national conventions instead of in congressional caucuses, and the Anti-Masonic Party held the first national nominating convention in 1831. By 1832 every state but South Carolina chose presidential electors by popular vote. Parties organized parades, rallies, and newspapers, and they rewarded loyal supporters with government jobs, which became known as the spoils system.

The election of 1824 helped to bring about these changes. Andrew Jackson won the most popular and electoral votes but not a majority of electoral votes, and the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams. When Adams named Henry Clay secretary of state, Jackson's supporters charged that a “corrupt bargain” had denied the will of the voters. Jackson won in 1828, and voter turnout rose from about a quarter of eligible voters in 1824 to more than half in 1828 and to about 80 percent in 1840.

sections.takeaway: Conventions, popular votes for electors, and mass campaigns made politics a mass activity.

sections.title: The limits of democracy

blocks.text: The expansion of democracy was limited by race and sex. Many states took the vote away from free African American men even as they gave it to all white men. New York required free Black men, but not white men, to own property in 1821, and Pennsylvania excluded Black men entirely in 1838. Only a few New England states allowed Black men to vote on equal terms. In 1807 New Jersey ended the voting rights that some propertied women had held. Women could not vote anywhere, and American Indians were not citizens.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Do not describe the period as universal democracy. Suffrage became broader for white men and narrower for many free Black men.

sections.takeaway: Voting rights grew for white men, but women, free Black men, and American Indians were largely shut out.

connections.title: A mass electorate and a new party system
connections.body: A larger electorate rewarded politicians who spoke for ordinary voters. Topic 4.8 follows Andrew Jackson, the Democrats, and the Whigs.
connections.transferQuestion: Why did political parties have more reason to campaign for voters once property requirements ended?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that a much larger group of voters had to be reached and persuaded, which rewarded organization, rallies, newspapers, and appeals to ordinary voters.
